title: Honest Scales, Generous Hands, and a City's Health
summary: The chapter opens in the marketplace, with the LORD's hatred of dishonest scales, and moves through pride and humility, the ruin that wickedness brings on itself, the effect of the righteous and the wicked on a whole city, and the uses of wealth. Generosity that seems to lose ends up gaining, hoarding that seems to gain ends up cursed, and the chapter closes with a tree of life and a warning that all receive their due.
story: Chapter 10 set the pattern of the collection: two ways, two kinds of people, two lines per saying. Chapter 11 carries the same contrast out of the household and into the public square. The concerns widen to trade, lending, neighbors, the city, and the nation. The righteous and the wicked are not only private characters here; they build up or tear down the town they live in (verses 10-11). The book is teaching the son of chapters 1 to 9 that the fear of the LORD has to show up at the scales and in the grain market, not only at home.
historical:
Israel's economy ran on weighed silver long before coins were common, and even when coinage spread in the Persian period, weighing remained normal practice. A merchant carried a set of stone weights in a bag and weighed the buyer's silver or the goods on a hand-held balance. Archaeologists have found many small inscribed stone weights from Judah in the later monarchy, and they vary slightly from one another, which shows how much room there was for cheating. The law forbade carrying two sets of weights, one heavy for buying and one light for selling (Deuteronomy 25:13-16; Leviticus 19:35-36), and the prophets attacked merchants who did exactly that (Amos 8:5; Micah 6:11). Verse 1 stands in that same line.

The sayings about the city (verses 10-11) and the nation (verse 14) reflect a society where a town's elders sat in council at the gate, where kings relied on advisers, and where famine was a recurring threat. Verse 26 pictures the grain dealer who holds back stock in a lean year, waiting for prices to climb while his neighbors go hungry. Such practices are well attested wherever grain was the staple and harvests were uncertain.
cultural:
Verse 22 draws on two things every first reader knew. Pigs were unclean animals under Israel's law (Leviticus 11:7), and a gold ring worn in the nose was women's jewelry; Abraham's servant gave one to Rebekah (Genesis 24:47). The picture is deliberately grotesque: a costly ornament wasted on a snout rooting in the mud. Beauty without discretion is not condemned as beauty; it is shown to be wasted.

Verse 15 refers to standing surety, which meant pledging to cover another person's debt if he defaulted. Proverbs warns against it repeatedly (6:1-5; 17:18; 22:26-27), especially for a stranger, because a man could lose his land or even his freedom for someone else's failure. That is not a ban on generosity, as verses 24-25 make plain; it is a warning against rash promises that put the family's livelihood at risk.
literary: Most of the chapter is again antithetical parallelism, but it holds several small clusters. Verses 3 to 8 all make the same point from different angles: righteousness delivers, and the wicked are caught by their own wickedness. Verses 9 to 14 turn to the effect of speech and counsel on neighbor, city, and nation. Verses 24 to 26 form a tight group on giving and withholding. Verses 1 and 20 both use the pair abomination and delight, bracketing much of the chapter with the LORD's own judgment. Verse 22 is the chapter's single comparison saying, built on like rather than but, and its shock value depends on the reader supplying the comparison. The chapter closes with a how-much-more argument (verse 31), a form of reasoning from lesser to greater.

outline.t: Surety, kindness, and the wages of the wicked
Beauty without discretion; desire and hope
Seeking good, trusting riches, and the tree of life

doctrines.note: Verse 1 applies the Torah's commands about honest weights to daily trade and calls fraud an abomination to the LORD, the same strong word the law uses for idolatry. Wisdom is not an alternative to God's law but the art of living it in ordinary transactions.

The chapter insists that wrongdoing does not escape: riches are worthless in the day of wrath (verse 4), the wicked will not go unpunished (verse 21), and all receive their due (verse 31). Much of that judgment works from within, as the wicked are trapped by their own desires (verse 6).

Pride (verse 2), contempt for a neighbor (verse 12), gossip (verse 13), cruelty (verse 17), and hoarding (verse 26) are all named. Sin in Proverbs is seldom abstract; it is a habit that damages people nearby and eventually the one who practices it.

words.note: To'evah, abomination or detestable thing. The word expresses deep revulsion. Elsewhere it names idolatry, pagan rites, and serious sexual sin, so its use for rigged scales (verse 1) and for the perverse in heart (verse 20) is startling. God is as offended by quiet commercial fraud as by open false worship.

Even, stone, here in the sense of a weight. Verse 1 literally speaks of a whole or complete stone as the LORD's delight. Deuteronomy 25:13 forbids having a stone and a stone in your bag, that is, two different weights for different customers. Honest measure was a matter of worship as well as business.

Ratson, favor, delight, acceptance. In Leviticus the word describes offerings that are acceptable to the LORD. Proverbs moves it into the marketplace: an accurate weight is his delight (verse 1), and so are the blameless in their walk (verse 20). What pleases God is not confined to the altar.

Chesed, kindness, often rendered steadfast love or loving devotion. In verse 17 the kind man is literally a man of chesed. The word usually describes loyal love within a relationship, including God's covenant faithfulness to Israel, and here it names a character that blesses others and, the saying adds, benefits the one who has it.

christ: Several of these sayings reappear in the New Testament. Verse 31 is quoted by Peter in the form it takes in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament made in the centuries before Jesus), where it speaks of the righteous being saved with difficulty and asks what will become of the ungodly (1 Peter 4:18). Peter applies it to Christians suffering for Christ's name. The sayings on generosity (verses 24-25) are close to Jesus' teaching that the measure you use will be measured back to you (Luke 6:38), and his parable of the rich fool who built bigger barns (Luke 12:16-21) is verse 28 told as a story. The tree of life in verse 30 recalls Eden and anticipates its return in Revelation 22:2. These are thematic links rather than predictions, but they show the New Testament reading Proverbs as a book about the same God and the same two ways that Jesus himself set before his hearers.

hard.q: What does verse 30 mean by saying that he who wins souls is wise?
hard.a:
The phrase has become familiar as a call to evangelism, but the Hebrew is more difficult than the English suggests. Literally it says that one who takes lives (or souls) is wise, and elsewhere to take a life usually means to kill (for example, Proverbs 1:19). Interpreters handle this in three main ways. Many read the phrase positively in context: the righteous person, like a tree of life, draws others in and wins them over, gaining their trust and bringing them toward life. Some modern translations follow the Septuagint, which reads the second line differently, and change one Hebrew word so that the line speaks of violence taking lives away, making a neat contrast with the first line. Others keep the Hebrew and suggest a wordplay: the wise capture people as surely as a violent man does, but for life rather than death.

What is clear is that the verse is not a technical instruction about evangelism; it is a saying about the life-giving influence of the righteous. Christians who apply it to sharing the faith are drawing a fair extension from that theme, provided they do not build too much on a phrase whose exact sense is uncertain.

questions: Verse 1 calls dishonest scales an abomination to the LORD. Where in modern work and business do the equivalents of two sets of weights show up?
Verses 24 and 25 say the generous gain and the withholder grows poor. Is this a promise of financial return, or a description of how generosity tends to shape a life and a community?
Verses 10 and 11 say a city is built up or torn down by its people. What does it look like for ordinary people to bless the town they live in?
